reasoning_traces.think:
The Bradley-Terry model defines a probabilistic framework where pairwise outcomes are governed by latent strengths γi. The core equation P(i≻j) = γi/(γi+γj) embeds a logistic link between differences in strengths. This formulation allows for efficient estimation via maximum likelihood, though it suffers from identifiability issues unless constrained (e.g., 1^T u = 0). In GSI, this translates to Bayesian inference over γi using conjugate gamma priors, enabling uncertainty quantification. For GSE, the model supports dynamic extensions through covariates xe,i that vary per edge, allowing contextual adjustments such as home-field advantage. The graph structure Hn(E) ensures comparability across all pairs, while its connectivity is essential for convergence of estimators. When the graph becomes disconnected, the model breaks down due to non-identifiability. The assumption of independent outcomes conditional on the graph is often violated in practice, especially in sports where outcomes may depend on unobserved variables. The model also assumes strong connectivity for MLE existence, which fails when some teams dominate others indefinitely. These limitations define the operational boundaries of the Bradley-Terry framework in real-world applications.
